sentences.text: Cycnorhamphus is a genus of gallodactylid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic of France and Germany, dating to approximately 152 million years ago.
This creature possessed a wingspan of approximately 135 centimeters.
It featured a unique beak shape that curved both upward and downward compared to other pterosaurs.
A specimen nicknamed "The Painten Pelican" reveals unusual peg-like teeth at the jaw tips that became blunter and stouter in older individuals.
The jaw anatomy includes curvatures forming an opening behind the teeth, occupied by two mineralized soft tissue structures from the upper jaw.
The type species was originally named Pterodactylus suevicus by Friedrich August Quenstedt in 1855 based on a fossil found near Nusplingen in Württemberg.
Harry Govier Seeley established the genus Cycnorhamphus in 1870 by reassigning Pterodactylus suevicus to it.
The genus name Cycnorhamphus is derived from Greek words meaning "swan" and "beak", referencing the animal's snout shape.
Felix Plieninger rejected the separation of Pterodactylus and Cycnorhamphus in 1907, a view held by most paleontologists for over sixty years.
Jacques Fabre named the species Gallodactylus canjuersensis in 1974 based on a specimen found in the Les Besson quarries near Aiguines, France.
Christopher Bennett argued in 1996 that Cycnorhamphus has priority over Gallodactylus, renaming the French species Cycnorhamphus canjuersensis.
Christopher Bennett formally synonymized Cycnorhamphus canjuersensis and Cycnorhamphus suevicus in 2010 and 2012, suggesting differences were due to age, sex, or individual variation.
Researchers speculate that Cycnorhamphus used its unique jaws to crush or bisect hard invertebrates like mollusks, similar to openbill storks.
Phylogenetic analysis places Cycnorhamphus within the family Gallodactylidae, as the sister taxon to Normannognathus.
Cycnorhamphus lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 152.21 and 145.06 million years ago.
